full_judgment:
M.H. Rahman, J.- The High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 14 June 1994 passed in Criminal Misc. Case No.715 of 1994 rejected the appellant's prayer for bail in connection with C.R. Case No.1364 of 1994 under section 295A of the Penal Code, pending in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. 

 3. On 8 June 1994 Md. Nurul Alam, Officer-in-Charge of Motijheel Police Station, Dhaka lodged a petition of complaint before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka under section 295A of the Penal Code against the writer of the column, the Editor and the Advisory Editor, and the Executive Editor of the Daily Janakantha. It was alleged, inter alia, that in the aforesaid article the verses of the Holy Quran were deliberately misinterpreted with a malicious intention to outrage the religious feelings of the Muslims. On that, complaint Criminal Case No.1364 of 1994 was started. By the impugned order the High Court Division rejected the appellant''s prayer for bail. 

 4. The appellant now contends that the High Court Division erred in law in not considering the principles of granting anticipatory bail and misdirected itself to a wrong enquiry as to whether there was any prima facie case against the appellant. It is submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in not considering the appellant's apprehension that he would not be granted bail by the learned Magistrate in view of the fact that two other co accused, the Advisory Editor and Executive Editor of the newspaper, had earlier been refused bail by the same Magistrate. 

 6. In Muhd. Ayub V. Muhd. Yaqub 19 DLR (SC) 38 (54)=PLD 1966 (SC)1003, (1022-1023) Hamoodur Rahman J.—:-as he was then, observed that "here can be no doubt that section 498 gives extended and wider powers to the High Court and the Court of Session but this power will no doubt normally be exercised in a reasonable and judicial manner taking into account the limitations placed by other provision of the Code upon subordinate authorities and that a rule founded on justice and equity will not be disregarded unless there be exceptional circumstances. But this is a self-imposed restriction and not a restriction imposed by anything contained in the Section. Normally this general salutary principle will no doubt be kept in view and will not be lightly departed from but this should not, in my view, be held to debar the High Court and the Court of Session from deviating from it in exceptional cases or as controlling the wide words of section 498 as a matter of construction of the section. This principle is invoked in aid more as a precaution against the indiscriminate grant of bail and not as a statutory clog upon the powers of these courts" I respectfully agree with the above views. 

 7. This is not a case of bail anticipating arrest. The warrant of arrest had already been issued against the appellant and ordinarily he ought to have first surrendered to the Court that issued the warrant before filing an application for bail before the High Court Division. The High Court Division rightly rejected the appellant's preposterous contention that as the prosecution was initiated at the instance of the Ministry of Home Affairs the learned Magistrate working under the supervision of the executive authority of the Government would feel embarrassed to grant bail to him. All Magistrates are independent in the exercise of their judicial functions. Article 116A of the Constitution takes care of this aspect of the independence of the judicial functionaries. 

 8. In this case the appellant instead of appearing before the learned Magistrate went straight to the High Court Division for bail. He was laboring under an apprehension that the learned Magistrate who had earlier refused bait to two co-accused, the Advisory Editor and the Executive Editor of the Newspaper was most likely to refuse to grant bail to him. Considering this aspect of the matter and, further, that the evidence as to the offending article, being on print, is not likely to be tampered with and there is little chance of the appellant's jumping the bail the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is hereby set aside. The appellant is permitted to continue on the same bail already granted to him. In the result, the appeal is allowed.
